forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridge used £37.691m of its own cash for 2025/26 capital spending, its outturn report says
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridge City Council met £37.691m of its capital financing in 2025/26 from internal borrowing, using its own cash balances to pay for capital spending instead of taking a loan. Its treasury management outturn report, which went to Cabinet on 16 November 2026, says the cash balances "were maintained to provide funding for capital expenditure".

The report gives two figures for average deposits. Its highlights section says deposit balances averaged £53.636m over the year. A table in section 7.2 gives overall average deposits of £73.48m for 2025/26, against £149.52m in 2024/25.

Part of the cash funds Cambridge Investment Partnership LLP, the council's housing development partnership. The report says the funding will be repaid as housing developments complete and sales receipts are realised.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridge's housing repair bills force £6.4 million cut to tenant investment
news_drafts.lead: Cambridge Council cut planned investment in its housing stock by £6.4 million in 2025-26 to meet compliance costs that exceeded budget by £6.9 million. Awaab's Law repairs for damp and mould, interim fire safety measures and void management each exceeded forecast by up to £2.3 million. The council also faces £1.561 million in additional spending to repair the Jesus Green riverbank, prompting it to earmark its entire £1.930 million underspend for asset compliance work. Separately, the council is increasing its maximum development loan to Cambridge Investment Partnership by £12 million to £30.5 million, driven by build cost inflation and slowing sales from the Iran war. The HRA capital contribution cut will require increased borrowing to fund future housing investment.

findings.headline: General Fund net income from commercial and service investments was £10,404k in 2025/26, against a budget of £16,176k.
findings.detail: The table shows the figure for 2024/25 as £14,725k. The paper does not explain the variance from budget, and the HRA line and the percentage of net revenue stream row in the same table are not consistent with the General Fund figures.
findings.matters: A shortfall in commercial income compared with budget is a pressure other councils with property and service investment portfolios will recognise.
findings.figures: £10,404k actual 2025/26; £16,176k budget 2025/26; £14,725k actual 2024/25; 64.75% of net revenue stream (42.33% budget)

findings.headline: No voluntary revenue provision was charged in 2025/26, and the cumulative total of such charges from previous years stands at £9,545,000.
findings.detail: The minimum revenue provision charged to the General Fund in 2025/26 was £702,489, calculated under the policy in the Treasury Management Strategy. The paper says voluntary provision is permitted to reduce future MRP charges.
findings.matters: Councils deciding whether to make voluntary debt repayment will compare their own choice with this one when setting MRP policy.
findings.figures: £702,489 MRP charged to General Fund; £9,545,000 cumulative voluntary revenue provision as at 31 March 2026; £0 voluntary provision in 2025/26
findings.quote: No voluntary revenue provision charges were made during 2025/26.

findings.headline: The council complied with all Prudential Indicators and operated within the prescribed limits throughout 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the council operated within the authorised and operational borrowing limits in its Treasury Management Strategy Statement. The outturn indicators are set out in Appendix C.
findings.matters: Confirmation of compliance with approved prudential limits is the baseline a finance director or lender checks before relying on the council's borrowing position.
findings.figures: Authorised limit for borrowing £600,000k; operational boundary for external borrowing £340,800k (budget £493,568k)
findings.quote: The Council complied with all Prudential Indicators approved by Council and operated within the prescribed limits throughout the financial year.

findings.headline: MUFG now expects an extended period of higher interest rates than in its previous forecasts, after the Bank of England cut Bank Rate to 3.75% in December 2025.
findings.detail: The paper says inflationary pressures, geopolitical uncertainty and energy market volatility could delay reductions in Bank Rate. MUFG's February forecast had anticipated a cut to 3.50% in June 2026 and to 3.00% by September 2027, but the paper presents the revised outlook.
findings.matters: A later expected rate path changes the value of fixed-rate deposits and the cost of replacement borrowing for councils planning to refinance.
findings.figures: 3.75% Bank Rate; 3.50% forecast June 2026 (February forecast); 3.00% forecast September 2027 (February forecast)
findings.quote: with an extended period of higher interest rates now expected compared to previous forecasts.

findings.headline: The investment portfolio is now concentrated in shorter-term deposits and money market funds, following MUFG advice that better value is available at the shorter end of the yield curve.
findings.detail: The paper says the change is intended to let the council respond quickly to changing market conditions. Longer-term investments continue to be held where they support wider council objectives, including the CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund.
findings.matters: A shift toward short-dated investments changes the council's exposure to reinvestment risk when rates fall, which is the scenario the paper's own forecast describes.
findings.figures: £15,800k in fixed-term deposits and £23,601k in variable-rate notice accounts at 31 March 2026, total £39,401k
